combination of forest and grassland. I didn't stratify for various reason=
s=20
and decided to wait and post-stratify or incorporate covariates if=20
possible.  It turns out the key species I=92m working with were all sight=
ed=20
within the forest patches.  I=92ve considered breaking up transects and t=
his=20
doesn=92t seem possible because the fragmentation is too great.  For=20
example, I frequently recorded individuals while walking transects throug=
h=20
grassland while I observed them in forest patches.  Almost all transects=20=

are in an irregular, fragmented combination of grassland and forest.  I=20=

have cover estimates for grassland versus forest for the area searched fo=
r=20
each transect, and I recorded the points along each transect where there=20=

was a change from forest to grassland anticipating this might help for=20=

stratification or developing covariates after the survey was completed.=20=
=20

an estimate of forested and grassland area for the entire study area=20

messages.subject: MRDS - using fitted detection function from previous analysis
messages.subject_clean: MRDS - using fitted detection function from previous analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am having difficulty using MRDS to estimate density / abundance
from a fitted detection function of a previous MRDS analysis using
Distance 5 release 2.

I am using MRDS to fit a detection function to a larger dataset to
predict detection probabilities in a smaller dataset to estimate the
densitiy and abundance. This is covered in the Distance 5.0 release 2
user's guide in chapter 10, p137. So far I have been able to run the
initial MRDS model and retain the R data file for the following
analysis that uses the R output for the model definition.

I am receiving the following error in the log when I attempt to run
the second estimate density / abundance from a fitted detection
function of a previous MRDS analysis:
** Error: Could not find the Method command in the model definition.  **

I have checked and reinstalled the R package 2.4.1 that is currently
supported for use with the MRDS library. I have reinstalled Distance
5.0 release 2 and checked the settings for use with R according to
the user's guide. I have checked the .RData workspace to make sure
the data is there for further analyses and it appears to be there. I
have run the MRDS using the debug mode for script logging and it
works for the initial MRDS analysis but halts on the second 'estimate
density / abundance from a fitted detection function of a previous
MRDS' analysis.

Has anyone got any ideas why it is not working for me? Or
alternatively, is there a script that I could follow or adapt to use
in R for MRDS using a previously fitted detection function? I have
little experience in scripting for R but am willing to pull it all
apart and start learning for this one.

I have had a search in the archives and haven't found anyhting yet,
but apologies if it has already been covered.

Cheers,

Alistair

Hi James, List,

I believe given your setting the best is to proceed as you suggested at=20
the end of your query. The density estimate you obtain, say D, will be=20
valid for the total area A (this assumes that the design was random with=20
respect to the two different habitats).  Hence, the estimated total=20
number of animals is N =3D DA (for the combined grassland + forest area).=
=20
If you want Df, the density in the forested areas alone (which cover an=20
area Af, which you already have calculated), it is simply obtained by=20
N/Af. This assumes that there are effectively no birds in grassland,=20
which from your description seems a fair assumption.

Hope this helps,

Tiago

messages.body_plain:
In my opinion, developing a set of intervals because of heaping of
distances caused by rounding should be based on an assessment of that
measurement process and not based on the observed data.  If you feel you
must use the observed data I would look at it combined or by observer
and not by habitat.  What you are interested in is the best way to bin
the data such that any measurement error is minimized.  I can't
understand how that would be a function of habitat.

Obviously, the better solution is to use a more precise measurement of
distance, so you are not stuck with this issue.

--jeff

The basic problem is that you are doing a bootstrap fitting 3 different
detection functions based on only 33 observations.  While this is
perhaps a sensible thing to do in general, to quantify the model
selection uncertainty in selecting among plausible detection function
models, it is going to be a bit tricky when you have relatively few
observations, especially for point transect data as you have here.  In
general, we recommend getting around 90+ samples for a robust analysis
of point transect data -- although clearly it depends on how wide the
true detection function shoulder is, and whether there are any other
problems (violations of assumptions, etc).  So, you should take all
analyses you do with such a small sample with a pinch of salt.

When you do a bootstrap resample with so few observations, many of the
bootstrap samples will have, by chance, almost no observations at all in
them.  So the results will be quite unreliable - and you might end up
with unreasonably wide confidence intervals.  Also, Distance sometimes
does not work with very few observations, so it might crash -- although
it shouldn't.  Actually in this case, after some debugging, I found that
it's crashing on a bootstrap dataset that has 46 observations in it, so
this isn't the problem here.

Despite my reservations about your small sample size, the half-normal
detection function fit to your original data looks quite nice and well
behaved, with a reasonably wide shoulder and smooth decline in estimated
detectability and good fit to the data.  One possible problem is that
you don't do any truncation.  So Distance truncates at the largest
observation distance, which in your case is 0.11.  However, the
estimated detection probability at this distance in the original data is
almost zero.  Instead it's better to truncate so that the estimated
detection probability at the largest distance is rather higher -- tends
to lead to more reliable estimation in general (see Intro to Distance
Sampling book, section 1.5.3 for example) and probably more reliable in
the Distance software too.  I tried truncating at 0.08, which leaves 31
observations but a more reasonable estimated detection probability at
this distance of about 0.1.  Perhaps a little more truncation might work
too, but I didn't want to further thin your few data!  Anyway, the
estimated density was quite similar (239 vs 229), but now the bootstrap
runs fine.

esoteric fixes.

output in the log file, I saw that the program crashes during the
bootstrap with the following message:

to find the maximum likelihood solution given some starting values.

inside the opimization was going wrong, but it's likely a numerical
overflow as it tries a silly value for a detection function parameter.

parameters, so they can't do this.

problems.  I then re-ran the bootstrap and it ran fine.

is such strong evidence in the original dataset than no adjustments are
needed with the half normal detection function.  So, I set up 4 models
in a new analysis: half normal with manual selection of 0 adjustments;

with manual selection of 1 simple polynomial of order 4; half normal
with manual selection of 1 Hermite polynomial of order 4.  I then put
starting values for all these parameters based on the maximum likelihood
estimates found for that model on the original dataset.  Re-running the
bootstrap, I again had no problems.
